They also contradict the new 'Energy comparisons' card on the same page, which says 'Above the nearest reference the page gives a multiple of at most about 10×; below it, a share of at least about 10%'. With the default 10 ft Rex, any density from about 10^18 kg/m³ up to the slider's top (10^30) shows the neutron-matter text with a huge multiple, about the top 12 of the slider's 29 decades. In the same view, the Weight tab's own ladder tile gives the correct wording for the same energy. Major stands: this is exactly what the brief set out to remove, and the page contradicts itself about it.

findings.title: The supernova-blast rung is firm, but its own notes record a published spread of about 10×
findings.location: research/final-energy.json energy_supernova_blast (low_si 5e43, high_si 2e44, no rough field); build-data.py rough_fact; gui-c-research.json decision 'Rough rungs'
findings.evidence: Fact notes: 'Janka: kinetic energies ranging from ≳10^50 erg to some 10^51 erg for SNe ... ordinary single events range from about 10^50 to a few 10^51 erg (Janka 2012) ... Typical value known to about 2x: at the edge of the rough-wording rule.' Fetched https://arxiv.org/pdf/1206.2503 (p. 12): 'CC events show a large diversity concerning their kinetic energy, ranging from ≳10^50 erg to some 10^51 erg for SNe'. The light-of-a-supernova rung was made rough on exactly this kind of event-to-event spread ('(1-10) × 10^49 erg across such events', low 1e42 to high 1e43). The blast instead records only the 'typical' 0.5–2 × 10^51, so hi/v = 2.0 and it stays firm. The page then says '1.2× a supernova’s blast (its flying debris)' and '45% of a supernova’s blast'. Rough wording would give 'roughly the same as' and 'roughly 40% of'.
findings.expected: A rung uncertain by more than about 2× gets only rough wording (brief). Two supernova rungs that vary between events should be treated the same way. The published spread (about 10^50 to 2 × 10^51 erg) runs 10× below the value used.
findings.fix: Set low_si to 1e43 J (Janka's ≳10^50 erg), or add rough: true with the reason in the notes ('Rough by judgement: ordinary events span about 10^50 to a few 10^51 erg, Janka 2012'). Update the 'Rough rungs' decision, the README's count ('Nine rungs are rough') and its list.

verdict.reasoning: Reproduced, including the source. The fact's own notes record that ordinary single events range from about 10^50 to a few 10^51 erg (Janka 2012). Janka's p. 12 says so, fetched below. Yet low_si/high_si hold only the 'typical' 0.5–2 × 10^51 erg, so value/low = 2.0 exactly and the rung stays firm. The ladder treats the same kind of uncertainty as rough elsewhere. Supernova light is rough on its event-to-event range ((1–10) × 10^49 erg). Krakatoa is rough by judgement because 'published figures span about 60x' although its own range is under 2×. The hurricane is rough because 'storms differ by a factor of a few'. By those precedents the blast, whose events span about 10× below the value used, should be rough too. This is the review brief's 'a range that hides a wider published spread (which would wrongly make a rung firm)'. Decision 2 ('typical range is exactly 2x') does not square with the Krakatoa and hurricane reasoning, so the decision is unjustified, not just a departure from the brief's letter. Page effect: firm wording such as '1.2× a supernova’s blast (its flying debris)' and '45% of ...' where rough wording would give 'roughly the same as' and 'roughly 40% of'.
verdict.reproduction: research/final-energy.json energy_supernova_blast: value_si 1e44, low_si 5e43, high_si 2e44, no 'rough' field. Its notes say 'ordinary single events range from about 10^50 to a few 10^51 erg (Janka 2012) ... Typical value known to about 2x: at the edge of the rough-wording rule.' Fetched https://arxiv.org/pdf/1206.2503 (pdftotext, p. 12): 'But CC events show a large diversity concerning their kinetic energy, ranging from ≳10^50 erg to some 10^51 erg for SNe and up to several 10^52 erg for HNe (Fig. 3).' 10^50 erg = 1e43 J, 10× below the value. Node: L.compare(1.2e44) = '1.2× a supernova’s blast (its flying debris)', L.compare(4.5e43) = '45% of a supernova’s blast (its flying debris)'. With rough:true on that rung: 'roughly the same as ...' and 'roughly 40% of ...'. The supernova-light fact for comparison: low 1e42, high 1e43, '(1-10) × 10^49 erg across such events', rough.
verdict.better_fix: In research/final-energy.json energy_supernova_blast, add `"rough": true` and append to notes: 'Rough by judgement (field rough): the typical value is known to about 2x, but ordinary core-collapse events span about 10^50 to a few 10^51 erg (Janka 2012, p. 12), as supernova light spans 10x across events.' (test/ladder.js needs the 'Rough by judgement' phrase.) Alternatively set low_si to 1e43 J (Janka's ≳10^50 erg), and the 2× rule makes it rough. Then update the 'Rough rungs' decision in research/reviews/gui-c-research.json, the README's 'Nine rungs are rough' (to ten) and its list, and rebuild.

findings.outcome: Fixed: rough by judgement (field rough), with Janka 2012 and Burrows & Vartanyan in the notes; README and decisions updated (ten rough rungs).

verdict.reasoning:
I reproduced this, and the gap is wider than the finding says. The branch's page has the sources-table row 'Energy: A lightning flash: total energy' with the value 'about 1 GJ per flash (published estimates 0.1 to 7 GJ)'. In final-energy.json, energy_lightning_flash has low_si 1e8, high_si 7e9 and notes that say 'span 70x'. Both ends come from four sources that are not independent: EPA repeats Borucki & Chameides.

(1) arXiv 2404.10020, fetched and extracted, says twice that a flash carries 10^9 to 10^10 J, citing Rakov & Uman 2003. Line 1497: 'A single cloud-to ground lightning flash has a total energy of the order of 10^9 to 10^10 J [Rakov2003].' Line 187: '...bearing 10^9 to 10^10 J in total [Rakov2003]'. I could not open the textbook itself: Internet Archive's search-inside for item lightningphysics0000rako returned 403.

(2) A stronger source that I fetched and read: Salinas, Bruning, Mansell & Brothers (2021), 'Modeling the Electrical Energy Discharged by Lightning Flashes Using Capacitors...', J. Atmos. Sci. 78:3909. It is refereed and open access. Its section 6a says past estimates 'have showed typical values ranging from 10^7 to 10^10 J of energy (Cooray 1997; Borovsky 1998; Marshall and Stolzenburg 2001)'.

So the published spread is about 0.01 to 10 GJ, wider than '0.1 to 7 GJ' at both ends. The page's claim about the literature is therefore too narrow. Nothing else changes. The rung was already rough (rough_fact: range more than 2x). The disaster skeptic listed this as open (gui-c-research.json, disaster, missing (3): 'EIA plant-level data would confirm whether an average year still means about 4 billion kWh'). I checked EIA-923 plant data for Hoover Dam NV (plant 154) plus AZ (plant 8902): https://api.eia.gov/v2/electricity/facility-fuel/data/?frequency=annual&data[0]=generation&facets[plantCode][]=154&facets[plantCode][]=8902&facets[fuel2002][]=ALL&facets[primeMover][]=ALL&api_key=DEMO_KEY . No year since 2002 reached 4.0 TWh. On the page, an energy equal to the last decade's average year (1.16e16 J) reads '81% of an average year of the Hoover Dam's electricity', and the last five years' average (1.08e16 J) reads '75% of ...'.
findings.expected: A firm rung labelled 'an average year', with no date, should match current averages within about 20%, or say which period it averages. The 4.0–4.2 billion kWh range is an average of years up to 2008, which the dam has not reached in any year since 2002.
findings.fix: Either date the rung: page_short 'an average year of the Hoover Dam's electricity before the drought (1947–2008)', with the label and display saying 'average to 2008'. verdict.reasoning: The data in the finding are correct, but they do not show a defect. The rung is 4.0e9 kWh (1.44e16 J), the figure USBR's live FAQ gives today in the present tense ('generates, on average, about 4 billion kilowatt-hours'). Combining USBR's 1947–2008 average (4.2 billion kWh over 62 years) with EIA-923 net generation for 2009–2025 gives a long-run 1947–2025 average of 4.04 TWh. That is the rung's value, so 'an average year of the Hoover Dam's electricity' is accurate as a long-run average, drought years included. The 2016–2025 mean is 3.23 TWh, 81% of the rung, which is inside the finding's own 'about 20%' test. Only the 2021–2025 mean (75%) falls outside it. The rung stays firm either way: the lowest year, 2023 at 2.7 TWh, is 1.5x below, not 2x. The sources table already shows the period ('1947-2008 average 4.2 billion kWh'), and the notes say post-2008 output was not checked. That open item is now closed in the rung's favour. Recent output really is lower, but that is useful context, not a wrong or mislabelled number.

findings.title: Beirut rung marked 'verified' though its sources disagree about 2x; the notes misread Pilger's infrasound figure as agreeing with 0.5 kt
findings.location: research/final-energy.json energy_beirut_explosion_2020 (status 'verified'; notes 'Value 0.50 kt, Rigby's published best estimate (Pilger's infrasound figure agrees)'); README.md known limits ('five rungs are disputed', Beirut not among them); sources-table row 'Energy: Beirut port explosion ...' shows 'verified'
findings.evidence: Pilger et al. 2021 (fetched as full text through Europe PMC: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC8266808/fullTextXML, the same article as the cited https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8266808/, which serves a reCAPTCHA to curl) says: 'For comparison, we account for more precise ECMWF profiles in the LANL relation we estimate a yield of about 0.5 kt TNT with a similarly large spread (0.14–1.12 kt TNT). However ... precise ECMWF profiles seem to be less appropriate for estimating yields with the LANL relation and will not be considered any further.' Pilger's retained infrasound results are 'Yield for AFTAC method (kt TNT) 0.86 0.86 1.47 1.06' and 'LANL (+HWM14) ... 1.05 0.22 1.35 0.86' (the last figure in each row is the average). Its damage fit says 'best explained by a yield of 0.8-1.1 kt TNT', and from the cargo 'a yield of about 1.4 kt TNT equivalent can be expected'. Rigby (https://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/id/eprint/165010/8/Rigby2020_Article_PreliminaryYieldEstimationOfTh.pdf) gives a best estimate of 0.50 kt and a reasonable upper limit of 1.12 kt. So the published central values are 0.5 kt (Rigby) against about 0.9–1.1 kt (Pilger), a factor of about 2. Krakatoa, whose 100–150 Mt against 200 Mt is a smaller disagreement, is marked 'disputed'.
findings.expected: By the house definitions ('disputed = sources disagree materially'), a value that one peer-reviewed study puts at 0.5 kt and another at about 1 kt is disputed, not verified. The notes should not cite as agreement an estimate the paper itself set aside.
findings.fix: Set the status to 'disputed', matching Krakatoa. In the notes, replace '(Pilger's infrasound figure agrees)' with: 'Pilger's retained infrasound estimates average 0.86–1.06 kt, its damage fit gives 0.8–1.1 kt, and it sets aside a 0.5 kt LANL+ECMWF variant.' Add Beirut to the README's list of disputed rungs (six, not five). The value 0.5 kt and the rough wording can stay.

verdict.reasoning: Reproduced. The fact's notes, and the merge decision in gui-c-research.json, say Pilger's infrasound estimate 'agrees' with Rigby's 0.5 kt. Pilger's own text gives the 0.5 kt LANL+ECMWF variant only 'for comparison' and then sets it aside: it 'will not be considered any further'. Pilger's retained infrasound averages are 1.06 kt (AFTAC) and 0.86 kt (LANL+HWM14). Its damage fit is 'best explained by a yield of 0.8-1.1 kt TNT', and it expects about 1.4 kt from the cargo. So two peer-reviewed studies of the same event give central values about 2x apart: 0.5 kt (Rigby) against about 0.9–1.1 kt (Pilger). The research applies 'disputed' to that kind of disagreement elsewhere: Krakatoa (100–150 Mt against 200 Mt) and SN 1998bw (Höflich against Iwamoto). The page's legend also defines disputed as 'contested'. Marking Beirut 'verified', while the notes cite a set-aside figure as agreement, overstates the evidence. The sources-table badge shows 'verified', and the README's 'five rungs are disputed' leaves Beirut out. The page's numbers are fine: the value and range are right, and the rung is already rough.

findings.title: Krakatoa note calls a GSA scientific volume 'a popular book', and 'the one refereed estimate' overstates the record
findings.location: src/app.html growthWhatIf firm.krakatoa (line 1958): 'Figures quoted in encyclopedias and a popular book run from about 10¹⁷ to 6.3 × 10¹⁸ J'; same text as 'the middle of the one refereed estimate'; README.md line 98 ('the one refereed estimate, from the air wave'); energy_krakatoa_1883 notes ('the only primary estimate'; 'its own range is the one refereed estimate')
findings.evidence: Lobanovsky 2013 Annex IV (https://arxiv.org/pdf/1311.6565): 'a book published by the American Geological Society says that «the energy of the largest natural explosion of historical time – the explosion of Krakatoa in 1883, is estimated to be 10^24 erg» [38], that is 10^17 joules'. His ref. 38 is 'E. Jones, J. Kodis – Atmospheric effects of large body impacts: The first few minutes. In: Geological implications of impacts of large asteroids and comets on the Earth. The Geological Society of America'. Google Books (id efz87W88HawC) shows that volume as edited by Silver & Schultz, ISBN 9780813721903, with GSA's permission. Library catalogues give it as GSA Special Paper 190 (1982), the papers of the Oct 1981 Snowbird conference sponsored by the National Academy of Sciences and the Lunar and Planetary Institute. It is a scientific volume, not a popular book. Choi et al. 2003 (refereed, NHESS) also states a figure (200 Mt), so Harkrider & Press is not the only refereed publication with a number. In app.html, README line 98 and the fact notes, say 'the one refereed estimate with a stated method (from the air wave)' instead of 'the one refereed estimate' or 'the only primary estimate'.

verdict.reasoning: Reproduced. The 10^17 J bottom of the quoted spread comes from Lobanovsky's ref. 38: Jones & Kodis, 'Atmospheric effects of large body impacts: The first few minutes', in GSA Special Paper 190 (1982), pp. 175–186.
